questions.question: In a three-tier campus design, which tier connects end-user devices?
questions.explanation: Access switches connect PCs, phones, and APs.

correct.explanation: The access tier connects end-user devices — PCs, phones, and access ports on switches/APs.

incorrect.explanation: Core provides high-speed backbone between distribution blocks — not direct end-user attachment.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Connecting users at the core tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Core describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given access tier, Access matches the tested behavior — Core applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Distribution aggregates access switches and applies policy — users connect at access, not distribution.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Placing user ports in distribution tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Distribution describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given access tier, Access matches the tested behavior — Distribution applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Spine is a data-center fabric term — campus three-tier uses access/distribution/core.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Mixing DC spine-leaf with campus access tier
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spine describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for access tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given access tier, Access matches the tested behavior — Spine applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Campus three-tier: Access = users. Distribution = policy/aggregation. Core = backbone.

questions.question: Spine-leaf architecture is primarily used for…
questions.explanation: Spine-leaf fabrics optimize predictable, scalable traffic between servers in data centers.

correct.explanation: Spine-leaf provides full bisection bandwidth for east-west (server-to-server) traffic in data centers.

incorrect.explanation: SOHO Wi-Fi uses a single AP/router — not a multi-spine fabric design.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying DC fabric to home Wi-Fi
incorrect.whatItDoes: SOHO Wi‑Fi describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given spine-leaf, Data center east-west traffic matches the tested behavior — SOHO Wi‑Fi applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Dial-up WAN is legacy remote access — unrelated to spine-leaf DC switching.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing WAN dial-up with DC architecture
incorrect.whatItDoes: Dial-up WAN describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given spine-leaf, Data center east-west traffic matches the tested behavior — Dial-up WAN applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Home gaming does not require spine-leaf — that architecture targets scalable DC east-west traffic.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using DC design for consumer gaming
incorrect.whatItDoes: Home gaming describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for spine-leaf.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given spine-leaf, Data center east-west traffic matches the tested behavior — Home gaming applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Spine-leaf = data center east-west scalability. Campus = access/distribution/core.

questions.question: Ten branch offices send all WAN traffic through headquarters. Which topology is this?
questions.explanation: All spokes via one hub = hub-and-spoke.

correct.explanation: All branches home through headquarters — classic hub-and-spoke WAN topology.

incorrect.explanation: Full mesh connects every site to every other site — not all traffic through one HQ hub.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing hub-spoke with full mesh
incorrect.whatItDoes: Full mesh describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given hub-spoke, Hub-and-spoke matches the tested behavior — Full mesh applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Spine-leaf is a data-center L2/L3 fabric — not the branch WAN pattern described.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying DC fabric to branch WAN
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spine-leaf describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given hub-spoke, Hub-and-spoke matches the tested behavior — Spine-leaf applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Point-to-point is one link between two sites — ten branches via HQ is hub-and-spoke.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Calling multi-branch HQ model point-to-point only
incorrect.whatItDoes: Point-to-point only describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for hub-spoke.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given hub-spoke, Hub-and-spoke matches the tested behavior — Point-to-point only applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: All branches → HQ = hub-and-spoke. Every site ↔ every site = full mesh.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of a full-mesh WAN?
questions.explanation: Full mesh connects every site to every other — resilient but expensive.

correct.explanation: Full mesh needs n(n−1)/2 links — cost and complexity explode as sites grow.

incorrect.explanation: Full mesh maximizes redundancy — the trade-off is cost/complexity, not lack of redundancy.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing mesh removes redundancy
incorrect.whatItDoes: No redundancy describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given full mesh, High cost/complexity for many links matches the tested behavior — No redundancy applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Mesh works over various transports — it is not limited to fiber only.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Restricting mesh to one media type
incorrect.whatItDoes: Only works with fiber describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given full mesh, High cost/complexity for many links matches the tested behavior — Only works with fiber applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Routing still runs over mesh links — mesh describes topology, not elimination of routing.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Thinking mesh removes routing protocols
incorrect.whatItDoes: Eliminates routing describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for full mesh.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given full mesh, High cost/complexity for many links matches the tested behavior — Eliminates routing applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Full mesh = max redundancy, max cost. Hub-spoke = cheaper, single point at hub.

questions.question: A collapsed core campus design has how many tiers?
questions.explanation: Two-tier merges distribution and core — access + collapsed distribution/core.

correct.explanation: Collapsed core merges distribution and core into two tiers: collapsed core + access.

incorrect.explanation: One tier would be a flat network — collapsed core still has access and a combined core/distribution layer.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Calling collapsed core a single-tier design
incorrect.whatItDoes: One describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given two-tier, Two matches the tested behavior — One applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Four tiers exceed standard collapsed-core models — collapsed means fewer tiers than classic three-tier.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Adding extra tiers to collapsed design
incorrect.whatItDoes: Four describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given two-tier, Two matches the tested behavior — Four applies a different mechanism.

incorrect.explanation: Five tiers is not a standard campus model — collapsed core reduces to two functional tiers.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Inventing non-standard tier count
incorrect.whatItDoes: Five describes a mechanism that could sound plausible for two-tier.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Given two-tier, Two matches the tested behavior — Five applies a different mechanism.

answerReview.examTip: Collapsed core = 2 tiers (access + collapsed core/distribution). Classic = 3 tiers.
